one_liner: Header-only C++11 thread pool with per-worker Vyukov MPMC queues; reposts jobs about 20x faster than an asio io_service pool.
what_it_does: A fixed-size pool of worker threads (default hardware_concurrency) where each worker owns a bounded lock-free queue (default 1024 slots, power of two). You call post(handler) or tryPost(handler) with a nullary callable; there is no future/result return, no wait or drain call and no parallel-for. Tasks are stored in FixedFunction<void(), 128>, a move-only std::function substitute with 128 bytes of inline storage.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker has its own Dmitry Vyukov bounded MPMC ring buffer (per-cell sequence numbers, one CAS per push/pop, cache-line padding), so a post from a worker thread goes to that worker's own queue with no shared lock. Posts from non-worker threads are spread round-robin with a relaxed atomic counter. FixedFunction avoids heap allocation per task. An idle worker steals one task at a time from a single fixed neighbour (worker i+1) and otherwise sleeps 1 ms.
when_to_use: Many tiny fire-and-forget tasks where std::function allocation and a mutex-guarded shared queue dominate cost
Tasks that repost continuations from inside workers (actor-style or chained callbacks), which stay on the local queue
Projects that want a small, dependency-free, header-only C++11 pool they can vendor and modify
Callables with captures under 128 bytes (static_assert enforced) or a custom FixedFunction size via ThreadPoolImpl
when_not_to_use: Latency-sensitive work after idle periods: idle workers poll with a 1 ms sleep, so wake-up latency is up to ~1 ms and idle threads burn CPU (issue #20)
When you need every posted task to run at shutdown: the destructor stops workers immediately and drops queued tasks (open issue #32, also #17 and #27)
Bursty producers: the per-worker queue is bounded, and post() throws std::runtime_error when the chosen worker's queue is full
Fork-join or recursive divide-and-conquer workloads: no join/wait primitive and stealing is from one neighbour only; use a real work-stealing scheduler (TBB, Taskflow, libfork) instead
Projects needing maintenance: last commit 2018-02-06, open issues include a deadlock when used as a global in a DLL (#29)

integration.dependencies: none (boost::asio only for the optional benchmark comparison; googletest for tests)
integration.platforms: any platform with std::thread and thread_local
integration.thread_safety: post/tryPost are safe from any thread (lock-free MPMC queues); construction, move and destruction are not thread-safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: post(handler) matches io_service::post in shape, but there is no run()/IO integration, no strand and tasks must be nullary and fit in 128 bytes

gotchas: All exceptions thrown by tasks are silently swallowed by a catch(...) in the worker loop.

Move constructors of ThreadPoolImpl, Worker and MPMCBoundedQueue are written as '*this = rhs;' with rhs a named rvalue reference, which cannot bind to the move-assignment operator; they fail to compile if instantiated, so treat the pool as non-movable.
Work stealing is a single ring: worker i only steals from worker i+1, one task at a time, from the FIFO end of an MPMC queue, so imbalance spreads slowly.
Queue size must be a power of two (>= 2) or the constructor throws std::invalid_argument; Worker::stop uses a relaxed store on the running flag.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over nexus or dp::thread_pool only when you need a tiny C++11-compatible, header-only fire-and-forget pool you will vendor and patch yourself; for fork-join or parallel-for, Fork Union, citor or a Taskflow/TBB-class scheduler are better documented and maintained, and nexus publishes comparisons against Taskflow and BS::thread_pool rather than an author-written asio pool.
verified_claims_summary: The README shows one example run of benchmark/benchmark.cpp: 16 concurrent chains each reposting a job 1,000,001 times, 61.7-70.3 ms per chain versus 1,381.6-1,393.2 ms with an author-written boost::asio io_service pool using hardware_concurrency threads (about 20x, derived from page data); no compiler, flags, Boost version or CPU are given. The workload favours this design: a repost from a worker lands in that worker's own lock-free queue, while the asio pool funnels everything through one shared io_service queue.
status_note: Abandoned since February 2018 (585 stars, 127 forks, not archived) with open bugs on shutdown task loss and DLL-global deadlock, but MIT plus BSD-2-Clause and about 600 lines, so it is easy to vendor and fix.
